caption_or_description: Dispersion by a prism makes the components of white light visible.
Dispersion of sunlight by a single raindrop.

Sunlight incident on two sample raindrops, as shown, emerges from them as dispersed light. The observer sees the red light from the upper drop and the violet light from the lower drop. Millions of drops produce the whole spectrum of visible light.

When your eye is located between the Sun (not shown off to the left) and a water drop region, the rainbow you see is the edge of a three-dimensional cone that extends through the water drop region. (Innumerable layers of drops form innumerable two-dimensional arcs like the four suggested here.)
Only raindrops along the dashed line disperse red light to the observer at a 42 degree angle; hence, the light forms a bow.

caption_or_description: Two refractions and a reflection in water droplets produce light at all angles up to about 42 degrees, with the intensity concentrated where we see the rainbow at 40 degrees to 42 degrees. No light emerges from the water droplet at angles larger than 42 degrees unless it undergoes two or more reflections inside the drop. So the sky is brighter inside the rainbow than outside it. Notice the weak secondary rainbow to the right of the primary.
